AWARD 


This is a petition filed U/Sec.2-A (2) of I.D. Act, 1947 praying to set aside the dismissal order 
dt.21/29.01.2025 issued by Respondent No.2 and to direct the respondents’-company to reinstate the petitioner into 
service with continuity of service, all other consequential attendant benefits and full back wages. 


2. The alpha and omega of the case of the petitioner is as follows:- 


2(a). The petitioner was appointed in the SCCL Company and taken to duty on 17.05.2017 as Badli-Worker under 
dependant employment scheme as his father late Sri Shankar died while in service. Ever since his appointment, the 
petitioner was discharging his duties to the utmost satisfaction of all his superiors and was promoted as General 
Mazdoor. He has put-in more than (100) musters per year and his year-wise musters of 2017 and 2018 are submitted 
here under:-

2(b). Further, mother of the petitioner Smt.Ch.Laxmi, suffered from serious ill-health and petitioner got imparted 
prolonged treatment to her in the SCCL and other referral hospitals. Due to demise of his father, petitioner has to look 
after his ailing mother Laxmi and could not attend his duties regularly. Further, due to prolonged stay in the hospitals 
on one hand and strenuous work in the underground mine, the petitioner’s health badly deteriorated. He took 
treatment at regular intervals in the SCCL dispensary, SCCL Area hospitals & other hospitals; but, his health 
condition was not improved and he suffered from severe ill-health. He continued to work in the underground on one 
hand and undergoing treatment on the other hand, his health completely deteriorated. But, without considering the 
true facts, chronic ill-health suffered by the petitioner and medical treatment imparted to him, the 2" respondent 
issued charge sheet dt.31.01.2023 alleging absenteeism from duty during the year 2022:- 


“25.25: Habitual later attendance or habitual absence from duty without sufficient cause”. 


2(c). There is no habitual late attendance or habitual absence from duty without sufficient case on the part of the 
petitioner, as alleged. There is reasonable and sufficient cause for his not attending to duties regularly during the 
charge sheet period. The charge sheet dt.31.01.2023 was served to the petitioner on 10.04.2023, to which he 
submitted his detailed written explanation on 12.04.2023. The respondents company imparted treatment to the 
petitioner in the SCCL Area Hospital and other referral Hospitals. He participated in the domestic enquiry on 
24.06.2021 and deposed the true facts of his ill-health and other problems faced by him, before the Enquiry Officer. 
The Respondent No.1&2 have concealed the above facts of ill-health and medical treatment imparted to the petitioner 
before the enquiry officer and suppressed the documentary evidence in favour of the petitioner. The findings of the 
Enquiry Officer are very cryptic and he gave his vague findings, which are quite biased and perverse. Without 
considering the true facts, the Respondent No.2 dismissed the petitioner from service vide Ref. dt.21/29.01.2025. 


2(d). The petitioner’s health condition was badly deteriorated and he suffered from serious ill health, during the 
charge sheet period. It is pertinent to submit that the petitioner was imparted treatment from 03.05.2023 to 
31.12.2024 by the SCCL Company. Further, the Medical Superintendent, KK-1 Dispensary, Mandamarri referred the 
petitioner to the Area Hospital, Ramakrishnapur, vide Reference Letter dt.02.01.2025. He was again referred by the 
Company Hospital to NIMS Hospital, Hyderabad for treatment of SCELEROTIC AORTIC VALVE, 
CARDIOMEGALY DISHIDEEMIA, for further evaluation and management vide Reference letter dt.25.01.2025, 
whereat he was imparted treatment. Further, the petitioner was referred to the SCCL Main Hospital, Kothagudem; he 
was reviewed on 25.02.2025, 11.03.2025 and 22.03.2025 and he was found FIT FOR DUTY, vide SCCL letter 
dt.24.03.2025. But, alleging absenteeism to duties during year 2022, the petitioner was dismissed from service ante- 
date vide Ref. dt.21/29.01.2025 unjustly, which is a clear case of victimization and unfair Labour practice. Thus, there 
is sufficient and reasonable cause for the petitioner for not attending to duties during the above charge sheet period. 
SCCL and other Medical documents may kindly be taken into consideration by this Court.

Officer by letter dt.10.08.2023, which was served to the petitioner on 05.01.2024 and he submitted written 
representation on 06.01.2024 itself. But, the Respondent No.2 straight away dismissed him from service vide Ref.

dismissal from service and he was not afforded an opportunity explain as to why the extreme punishment of dismissal 
shall not be imposed on him. It is highly arbitrary, against the principles of natural justice and is a clear case of 
victimization and unfair Labour Practice. The petitioner’s health condition badly deteriorated and he suffered from 
serious ill health, during the charge sheeted period and there is sufficient and reasonable cause for the petitioner for 
not attending to duties during charge sheet period and it cannot be termed as misconduct. 


2(f). Further, imposing the capital punishment of dismissal from service on the petitioner without any prior show 
cause notice proposing the said capital punishment is against the settled Law and contrary to the principles of natural

amounts to his economic death. Ever since his dismissal from service, the petitioner is out of employment and could 
not secure any other alternative job in spite of his best efforts. He hails from a very poor family and has no other 
source of livelihood. Therefore, he prays to set aside the dismissal order issued by the Respondent No.2 and to direct 
the Respondents’-Company to reinstate him into service with continuity of service, all consequential attendant 
benefits and full back wages.

3(c). The averments made by the Petitioner that he took treatment in the SCCL & other Hospitals at regular intervals 
and that his health condition was not improved and he suffered from chronic ill-health are false and denied. He was 
examined and certified “Fit for Duty” by the respondent company hospitals vide certificates issued on 23.11.2021, 
08.07.2022, 16.12.2022, 24.04.2023, 13.01.2024 and 23.03.2024. The medical treatment and referrals were standard 
administrative procedures necessitated by his prolonged unauthorized absenteeism, to determine his fitness status, 
before resume to duty. The averments made by the petitioner in his petition are false and baseless. He was given full 
and fair opportunity and natural justice principles were followed during the enquiry proceedings. He was warned that 
if he failed to meet the attendance requirements during 3-months observation period, suitable disciplinary action will 
be taken against him. This serves as a final show cause notice and was duly acknowledged by him. His failure to 
attend a single day during final observation period from 01.04.2024 onwards, proved his unwillingness to improve, 
leaving dismissal as the only course of action. 


3(d). Further, during brief administrative transition period from dismissal to name removal, he was referred to NIMS 
hospital and subsequently to the Main hospital, Kothagudem, where he was ultimately certified as “Fit for Duty”. He 
failed to attend work even once during final review period, demonstrating a complete lack of interest in his job. His 
CMPF amount of Rs.2,10,152/- was settled and Gratuity amount of Rs.2,58,583/- sanctioned and it is under process. 
The respondent company’s standing orders do not speak about of issue of Show cause notice proposing the 
punishment to be imposed on the delinquent employee. There is no victimization and the punishment of dismissal is 
not harsh and the petitioner was given number of opportunities to correct himself and to be regular to his duties by 
imposing minor penalties. But, he has failed to improve his attendance and resorted to unauthorizedly absent for duty. 
The petitioner’s misconduct compelled the Respondent/ Management to impose the penalty of dismissal which cannot 
be termed as unjust. 


3(e). Further, the Respondent Company employs more than 43,600 persons and the production results will depend 
upon the overall attendance and performance of every individual. If anyone remain absent without prior sanction of 
leave or without any justified cause, the work to be performed get effected. Such unauthorized absence creates 
sudden void, which at times is very difficult to fill-up with substitute, and there will be no proper planning and 
already planned schedules get suddenly disturbed without prior notice. For that reason every time the company 
inform its workers to intimate prior to the unit in-charge so that they may arrange substitute and failing to inform will 
result in to production and burden on other employees. The Respondent/ Management cannot be held responsible for 
the alleged debts and unemployment and the other allegations of the petition are denied and hence the Respondents 
prayed to dismiss the petition, without granting any relief to the petitioner.

8. Here, the learned standing counsel for the respondents’-company has strenuously argued and raised a Preliminary 
Objection in the Counter that since the coal mining industry is a central subject the Appropriate Government for 
Respondent/ Management is Central Government, which established Central Govt. Industrial Tribunal, at Hyderabad 
for adjudication of Industrial Disputes and the petitioner ought to have approached the said Tribunal for the redressal 
of grievance, if any. But, the Petitioner conveniently avoided filing his petition before the Tribunal established by the 
Central Government and approached this Tribunal; hence it is not maintainable under law and the same may be 
dismissed on this ground alone.

objection; has put forth and set forth that the petitioner was appointed as Badli Worker on 22.04.2017 and he being an 
underground employee is expected to put minimum 190 Musters in a calendar year. But, he was not regular to his 
duties and in only one year of 2018 he had put in the required 190 musters. The contentions of the Petitioner that he 
suffered from chronic ill-health and SCELEROTIC AORTIC VALVE, CARDIOMEGALY DISHIDEEMIA is incorrect. 
If he was really suffering from ill health, it becomes his primary responsibility to report sick in Colliery Hospital or he 
should have informed to unit officers about his incapability to attend duties and he would have got leave or loss of 
pay leave but he did not inform anything. The Respondent Company employs more than 43,600 persons and the 
production results will depend upon the overall attendance and performance of every individual. If anyone remain 
absent without prior sanction of leave or without any justified cause, the work to be performed get effected. Such 
unauthorized absence creates sudden void, which at times is very difficult to fill-up with substitute, and there will be 
no proper planning and already planned schedules get suddenly disturbed without prior notice. For that reason every

officer did not properly appreciate the documentary and oral evidence and he gave his vague findings, which are quite 
biased and perverse. The 2™ respondent required the petitioner to make representation on the findings report of the 
Enquiry Officer by letter dt.10.08.2023, which was served to the petitioner on 05.01.2024 and he submitted written 
representation on 06.01.2024 itself. But, 2" respondent straight away dismissed him from service vide 
Ref.No.MMR/PER/D/072/25/445, dt.21/29.01.2025. No prior Show Cause Notice was issued to the petitioner 
proposing the capital punishment of dismissal from service and he was not afforded an opportunity explain as to why 
the extreme punishment of dismissal shall not be imposed on him. The petitioner’s health condition was badly 
deteriorated and he suffered from serious ill health, during the charge sheeted period and there is sufficient and 
reasonable cause for the petitioner for not attending to duties during charge sheet period. 


[भाग पए---ख एण्ड 3(1i)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 973 


9c). The learned counsel for the Petitioner/workman further put forth and set forth that imposing the capital 
punishment of dismissal from service without any prior show cause notice is against the principles of natural justice. 
The extremely harsh punishment of dismissal is highly excessive and shockingly disproportionate, which amounts to 
economic death of the petitioner. Ever since his dismissal from service, the petitioner is out of employment and could 
not secure any other alternative job in spite of his best efforts. He hails from a very poor family and has no other 
source of livelihood. Therefore, he prayed to set aside the dismissal order and to direct the Respondents’-Company to 
reinstate the petitioner/workman into service with continuity of service, all consequential attendant benefits and full 
back wages. 


POINT No.1: 


10. Here, on the point of territorial jurisdiction of this Tribunal, it is settled Law that as per the Division Bench 
Judgment of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 1997(IID)LLJ(Supp.)11, Between: U. Chinnappa Vs. Cotton 
Corporation of India, this Tribunal has got every jurisdiction to entertain the Industrial Dispute raised by the 
petitioner/workman who was an employee of Singareni Collieries Company Ltd., Even though, the Central Govt. is 
appropriate Govt., for the respondents’-Company, the petitioner need not compulsorily raise the Industrial Dispute 
before the Central Govt. Industrial Tribunal, Hyderabad, as contended by the respondents’ company; and he can file 
this 1.10. case before this Tribunal as well. Hence, the contentions of the respondents’-company on the point of 
jurisdiction of this Tribunal are not sustainable under Law. Accordingly, it is answered in favour of the petitioner and 
against the respondents’ Singareni Collieries Company Limited. 


11. Further in this matter, initially the petitioner/workman denied the validity and legality of the enquiry report. 
But on 20.01.2026, the learned counsel for petitioner filed Memo U/Sec.11-A of ID Act by accepting the procedure 
of domestic enquiry to be fair and valid. Hence, it can be said the Enquiry Officer has followed the principles of 
natural justice. Now the next question is, whether the misconduct is proved in the facts of the case and the findings 
are not perverse. So, this Tribunal is to re-appreciate the evidence and come to its own conclusion with regard to 
finding guilty or not based on evidence. Accordingly, the Point No.1 is answered. 


POINT No.2 & 3: 


12. In view of the pleadings of the Petitioner/Workman as well as Respondents/corporation as well as in view of the 
rival arguments of their respective counsel now this Court will go into the evidence on record. Admittedly, the 
petitioner was dismissed from service by Proc. dt.21/29.01.2025 wherein it is alleged that the petitioner was absent 
from duty without sanctioned leave or sufficient cause during the year 2022. From a perusal of the record, it shows 
that Charge Sheet dt.31.01.2023 was issued to the petitioner, which is marked as Ex.M-8. It is evident from the charge 
sheet that the petitioner absented to duties for 341-days and put-in only 02 actual musters during the year 2022. It is 
further evident from the charge sheet under Ex.M-8 that he put in 126-musters during the year 2017, 192-musters 
during the year 2018, 19-musters during the year 2019; 07-musters during the year 2020 and 21-musters during the 
year 2021. Domestic enquiry was conducted and the enquiry proceedings are marked as Ex.M-9. Further, a perusal of 
Ex.M-9 proceedings of enquiry and enquiry report would goes to show that the Petitioner/Workman participated in 
the domestic enquiry and deposed that he remained absent on the dates as mentioned in the charge sheet and it was his 
mistake. He admitted that charges and pleaded guilty and deposed that due to his own health problems and his 
mother’s health problems, he did not attend to his duty. He accepted his mistake for remaining absent during the 
charge sheet year of 2022 and assured that he will be more careful in future and he will not remain absent without 
prior sanction of leave. 


12(a). From the Enquiry Report which is also under Ex.M-9, it is evident that the petitioner absented to duty without 
sanctioned leave and he accepted the charge made under Company’s standing order 25.25 (habitual late attendance or 
habitual absence from duty without sufficient cause) mentioned in the charge sheet dt.31.01.2023 was held proved. 
The petitioner has not submitted any documents regarding his mother’s health problems in the enquiry to substantiate 
his claim. Further, 7-days notice dt.10.08.2023 was issued, which is marked as Ex.M-10 and he was kept under 3- 
months observation period from 01.04.2024 onwards requiring put-in 16-UG musters per month and altogether 48- 
UG musters in 3-months time, which is marked as Ex.M-11. Another charge sheet dt.31.01.2024 was issued for his 
absenteeism during the year 2023 which is marked as Ex.M-12. The dismissal order dt.21/20.01.2025 is marked as 
Ex.M-13 wherein it shows that the petitioner received the enquiry report and proceedings on 05.01.2024. In turn he 
submitted written representation dt.06.01.2024, which was also considered to be not satisfactory. Hence, petitioner 
was dismissed from services of the Company with immediate effect. 


12(b). Further, attested copies of “Fit for Duty” letters dt.15.11.2024, 23.03.2024, 22.04.2023, 08.07.2022, 
13.01.2024 and 16.12.2022 filed by the Respondents/Company are marked as Ex.M-14 to Ex.M-19. It is evident that 
the petitioner was sent to the SCCL Main Hospital, Kothagudem and other Area Hospitals of SCCL for fitness. The 
petitioner was reviewed by the concerned SCCL Hospital and found made fit for duty. 


13. Apart from the above, the petitioner/workman submitted as many as 47 documents, medical prescriptions, medical 
reports and treatment imparted to him and his mother Laxmi. They are marked as Ex.W-4 to Ex.W-50. Most of the 
medical documents submitted by the petitioner/workman were issued by the SCCL Hospitals, NIMS, Kamineni, 
CHAIMS Hospital and other referral Hospitals, which prima-facie show that both the petitioner/workman and his 


974 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


mother Laxmi have suffered from ill-health for 5-years from 2019 to 2024. The petitioner explained that due to his ill- 
health and health problems of this mother, he absented to duties during the charge sheeted year of 2022 and prayed to 
consider his case sympathetically. Further, it is evident from the Pay sheets of petitioner under Ex.W-2 and Ex.W-3 
that he put-in 126-musters during the year 2017 and 192-musters during the year 2018. Thus, it is evident from the 
enquiry proceedings and enquiry report under Ex.M-9 as well as the material on record, that the petitioner had not put 
in minimum required musters of 190 during the year 2022. For which, petitioner submitted that due to his ill-health 
and health problems of his mother, he was unable to perform duty regularly during the charge sheet period and 
submitted several medical prescriptions and reports of SCCL and other referral hospitals, which are marked as Ex.W- 
4 to Ex.W-50. Further, the above medical documents of the petitioner lend support to his enquiry statement under 
Ex.M-9 showing the ill-health suffered by him and his mother. These documents clearly show that the petitioner/ 
workman and his mother both were imparted treatment during the charge sheet period. Hence, the defense put-forth 
by the petitioner is plausible and amount to mitigating circumstances. 


13(a). However, it is clear that the petitioner has not attended to duties during the charge sheet period and the charges 
were amply proved against him. Therefore, it can be said that the respondents/ company has no axe to grind against 
the petitioner. Hence, this Tribunal has no hesitation to hold that the charge leveled against the petitioner/ workman is 
proved and misconduct of the workman is established basing on the evidence and the findings of enquiry officer are 
not perverse. But, at the same time much gravity cannot be attributed to the petitioner since his ill-health and ill- 
health of his mother and treatment imparted by SCCL and other referral hospitals is supported by the medical 
documents, which shows reasonable cause for the petitioner’s absence during the charge sheet period. 


14. Now the question is whether the punishment of removal from service is disproportionate or not? 


14(a). It is settled law that the object of I.D.Act is to give succor to weaker sections of the society and it is a social 
welfare legislation. Here, there is no “Plumbline Precision” for deciding the proportionality of punishment, which 
depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court is empowered to 
exercise discretionary powers Under Sec.11-A of Industrial Disputes Act for judicious adjudication of the industrial 
disputes. Several factors like nature of duty, past service past conduct, previous penalties if any and the discipline 
required to maintain in the department, victimization and plea of the petitioner/workman and the punishment must be 
commensurate with the gravity of charges against the petitioner/ workman etc., by considering the relevant factors 
and mitigating circumstances of each case are to be taken into consideration so as to mould the relief appropriately 
and reduce the punishment imposed on the workman. 


15. Here, the learned counsel for the petitioner/workman submitted that the Petitioner was appointed in the year 2017 
as a dependant of his deceased father who died while in service and put in more than 100 musters for two years. The 
petitioner submitted the referral letters issued by SCCL Hospitals and the respondents have referred the petitioner to 
NIMS, CHAIMS, Kamineni and other Hospitals during the years 2019-2024. It appears from the medical documents 
submitted by the petitioner that he was imparted treatment for: “SCELEROTIC AORTIC VALVE, CARDIOMEGALY 
DISHIDEEMIA.”’ Further, the petitioner hails from a very poor family, he has got no other livelihood and facing 
untold financial problems, and prayed to consider the case U/Sec.11-A of I.D. Act. Here, the learned counsel for the 
petitioner relied upon the following citations:- 


1) HON’BLE SUPREME COURT JUDGMENT REPORTED IN AIR 1988 SC 303 — Between: Scooter India 
Ltd, Labour Court, Lucknow & ors: 


In this case, the Labour Court while holding that enquiry had conformed to statutory prescriptions and principles 
of natural justice, yet held that order of termination was not justified and ordered for reinstating employee 
with 75% back wages. Wide powers are vested in Labour Court or Tribunal. Labour Court can temper justice 
with mercy and give an opportunity to an erring workman to reform himself. Order of Labour Court granting 
relief of reinstatement with 75% back wages was upheld by Hon’ble Supreme Court. 


2) HON’BLE HIGH COURT JUDGMENT IN W.A. No.1101/2008 and W.P.No.7671 of 2000, dt.07.04.2009 
D.B. Judgment: 
In this case, the Labour Court granted reinstatement with continuity of service and half-of back wages. The 


Hon’ble High Court held that since the petitioner remained unemployed from the date of removal, modified 
the award of Labour Court by granting full back wages. 


3) Judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court, dt.24-08-2009 in Civil Appeal No.5762 of 2009, Between: Coal India 
Ltd. & Anr Vs. Mukul Kumar Choudari and others. 


4) Judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court dt.14-05-2009 Between: Jagadish Singh Vs. Punjab Engineering 
College and others. 


In the above Judgments of the Hon’ble Supreme Court at SI.No.3 & 4 reveals that the punishment should be in 
commensurate with the gravity of the charges and it should not be shockingly disproportionate. Further, this 
Tribunal is adhering to the ratio laid down by their Lordships as applicable to the facts of the present case on hand, 
to the extent of reinstatement only. 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 975 


16. Here, this Tribunal relied on a Division Bench Judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court rendered in Civil Appeal 
No.2157/1999, dt.08.04.1999 between Ajaib Singh vs. Sirhind Co-op. Marketing-cum-Processing Service Society 
Ltd., & another, wherein their lordships held that:- 


“The object of Industrial Disputes Act was to give succor to weaker sections of the society. The emerge 
Welfare State implies an end to exploitation of workman and as a corollary to that collective bargaining c 
Legislature had intended to protect workmen against victimization and exploitation by the employer and to 
Industrial Disputes in a peaceful manner. 


“The object of the Act, therefore, is to give succor to weaker sections of the society which is a pre- 
requisite for Welfare State. To ensure industrial peace and pre-empt industrial tension, the Act further aims at 
enhancing the industrial production which is acknowledged to be life-blood of a developing society. The Act 
provides a machinery for investigation and settlement of industrial dispute ignoring the legal technicalities 
with a view to avoid delays, by specially authorized Courts which are not supposed to deny the relief on 
account of the procedural wrangles”. 


16(a). Further, in a decision of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 2012 (1) ALD 220 (DB), wherein their lordships 
observed that:- 


“The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is a social welfare legislation, which required to be interpreted 
keeping in view the goals set out in the Preamble and Directive principles of State Policy in Part-IV of 
the Constitution. The Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal is conferred with very wide discretion U/Sec.11- 
A of the Act for granting appropriate relief”. 


17. Here, their Lordships of the Hon’ble Gujarat High Court in a case rendered on 04.05.1994, Between: Management 
of Glaxo India Ltd., Vs. State of Assam and 3 others categorically observed that “a Labour Court is required to settle 
a dispute according to the principles of natural justice, equity and good conscience and law without attaching 
undue importance to legal technicalities”. 


18. Further, it is well settled law that if the Industrial Tribunal/ Labour Court is satisfied that the punishment imposed 
on the petitioner/workman is not justified, the Industrial Tribunal/ Labour Court is clothed with the power to 
reappraise the evidence in the domestic enquiry and satisfy itself whether the said evidence relied on by the Enquiry 
Officer or Respondents/ Management established the misconduct alleged against the workman. Further, Section 11-A 
comes into effect only at the time when the Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court consider about the punishment to be 
imposed. While previously the Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court had no power to interfere with the punishment, it is 
now clothed with such a power. Apart from the above, Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court should temper justice with 
mercy and not flog the petitioner/ workman to asset our might. The power of ocean does not lie in its tumultuous tides 
but in its meditative vastness”. My above view is fortified with the observation of their Lordships of Hon’ble Madras 
High Court in a case Between: High Court of Madras Vs. R.D.Santhana Krishnan dt.21“ December, 2021. 


19. Here, it is to be noted that the concept of Industrial Dispute is quite broad and with the passage of time its horizon 
is being expanded. Further, the disputes are required to be resolved for the purpose of establishing peaceful and 
cordial atmosphere in an industry. Peace and harmony are the quintessential aspects which are to be kept in view 
while dealing with the “lis” or “controversy” relating to any industry. Apart from the above, whether the impugned 
punishment is so disproportionate as to shock the conscience of the Court, has to be decided on the facts of each case, 
having due regard to the gravity of misconduct & nature of duties discharged by the delinquent employee. 


20. Here, it is pertinent to note that the term “misconduct” is the intentional doing of something which the doer knows 
to be wrong, or which he does recklessly, not caring what the result may be. It includes negligence or want of proper 
care which an employee is to take. But, it is a fact that “to err is human” and “to forgive is divine”. Keeping the said 
spirit into consideration and in the interest of cause of justice, every errant conduct of an employee of an organization 
could not be treated as grave misconduct. Further, it is settled law that promoting empathy and understanding by 
encouraging forgiveness, which is a divine quality transcending human limitation, should be preferred to anything 
else in the given circumstances. My above view is fortified by observation of their Lordships of the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court in a judgment rendered Between: Ratilal Jhaverbhai Parmar Vs State Of Gujarat dt.21" October, 2024. 


21. Further, the Hon’ble Madras High Court observed in a case rendered in Management of Hyudai Motor India Ltd 
Vs. T.Sudhakar ... on 31" January, 2022: 


“When scales of justice stands balanced in a given case, the tilt to be exercised should be in favour 
of the poor workmen rather than the mighty Managements.” 


22. Therefore, by taking a holistic view of the matter, I am of the considered view that the extreme punishment of 
removal imposed by the respondents/corporation against the petitioner/workman is harsh, disproportionate and shocks 
to conscience of this Tribunal, hence, deserves to be modified since the disciplinary authority cannot be permitted to 
act arbitrarily and work like a Roman Knight and it cannot be allowed a fight between David and Goliath as in the 
present case on hand. Moreover, facts of this case attracts the proverbial saying “Every saint has a past and every 
sinner has a future” and Biblical proverbs “Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights of all 


976 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


who are destitute” and “Speak up and judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy.” Further, “Heavens 
would not have fallen if one more opportunity is given for the petitioner”. 


23. This Tribunal has perused, analyzed and meditated upon the case at hand, the case laws and principles of law 
referred above. In view of the above facts and circumstances and keeping in view of the principle “temper justice with 
mercy” and to meet the ends of justice, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the punishment of removal from service 
imposed on the petitioner is disproportionate and shocks the conscience of this Tribunal and hence, it deserves to be 
modified appropriately. It appears from the record that the petitioner rendered service of 7-years only in the 
respondents’ company and he is out of employment ever since his dismissal from service. Hence, this Tribunal is of 
the considered view that denial of entire back wages, continuity of service and all other attendant benefits during the 
intervening period from the date of his dismissal to till date and further “Deferment of Annual Increments for a 
period of TWO years with cumulative effect” would be a deterrent punishment to the petitioner. However, the past 
service rendered by the petitioner shall be protected and counted for all purposes. Hence, the punishment of dismissal 
from service imposed by the Respondents’ Company is hereby modified. Accordingly, the Points 2 & 3 are 
answered. 


24. IN THE RESULT, the petition is partly allowed. The dismissal order dt.21/29.01.2025 under Ex.M-13 issued by 
the Respondent No.2 is hereby modified. The respondents’ company is directed to reinstate the petitioner into service, 
but without any back wages, without any continuity of service and without any attendant benefits during the 
intervening period from dismissal till date and it shall be treated as “not on duty” for all purposes. However, the past 
service rendered by the petitioner shall be protected and counted for all purposes. Further, his Annual Increments 
shall be deferred for a period of TWO years with cumulative effect”. The petitioner is entitled to the salary only 
from the date of publication of the Award. Copy of the Award be sent to the appropriate Government for publication. 
Both parties shall bear their own costs.

order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a workman 
raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file written statement 
before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must also produce evidence 
to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce evidence, the dispute referred

This petition under Section 2 (A) (2&3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 as amended by the Amendment 
Act, 2010 filed by the petitioner workman against his termination with the case that he was first appointed as Cluster 
Incharge with the Management vide order dated 11.04.201land was posted at Datiya Gwalior Zone (M.P.). He 
successfully completed his probation period and thereafter, he was transferred from Datiya Gwalior Zone to Shajapur 
Ratlam Zone. As his work was nowhere supervisory or Managerial in nature, the Respondent No. 4 was the 
immediate Boss of the petitioner made some illegal demands which the petitioner showed inability to fulfil, he 
threatens the petitioner to spoil his career. The petitioner was transferred from Datiya Gwalior Zone to Shajapur 
Ratlam Zone. The petitioner was sick at that time and was not in a position to join at the new place of his posting. He 
submitted his application for medical leave which was sanctioned by Authorities and he also requested for 
cancellation of his transfer which was not accepted. Since, his transfer was mala fide and in form of his victimization, 
he raised a dispute before the Conciliation Officer in State Government. The Management terminated his services 
vide order dated 15.11.2018 on the ground that they have lost confidence in the petitioner which amounts to 


994 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


misconduct. This termination was without any show cause notice or any charge sheet initiating Departmental Enquiry, 
hence it is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. This act of Management amounts to retrenchment of services of the petitioner. 
Hence is in violation of Section 25F and 25G of the Act. The petitioner has prayed that setting aside his termination as 
it is vitiated in law, he be reinstated with back wages and consequential benefits. 


Due to absence of Management, the petition proceeded ex-parte against them. The petitioner had filed 
affidavit as his examination-in-chief and proved Exhibit W-1 to W-9 to be referred to as and when required. 

During the proceedings, the Management appeared and on their application, order to proceed ex-parte was 
set-aside on cost. Their written statement of defense was taken on record and case proceeded. 


The Management has taken a case that, firstly, the petitioner is not a workman under Section 2-S of the Act 
because he was a cluster in-charge drawing wages more than 40,000/- per month and was responsible for execution, 
operation and maintenance in Managerial and administrative capacity and Secondly, he was absenting himself un 
authorizedly and wilfully without permission of the Management and did not report on the place which he was 
transferred, hence Management was left with no option but to terminate his services. 


The petitioner did not appear for cross-examination by Management, in the light of his affidavit 
examination in chief. Management did not file any affidavit rather they filed the appointment letter and termination 
letter of the petitioner. 


At the stage of argument also, none appeared for petitioner. I have heard argument of Learned Counsel Mr. 
Jaideep Bansal for Management and have gone through records. 


It is worth mentioning that during the proceedings, the Management for Bharti Infratel was taken over by 
Indus Towers Limited and they were substituted in place of Bharti Infratel during the proceedings. 


The main objection raised by Management with regards to Maintainability of the petition is that, the 
petitioner is not a Workman as defined under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


The relevant provisions are being reproduced as under: 


2(s) “workman” means any person (including an apprentice) employed in any industry to do any manual, 
unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, whether the terms of 
employment be express or implied, and for the purposes of any proceeding under this Act in relation to an 
industrial dispute, includes any such person who has been dismissed, discharged or retrenched in connection with, 
or as a consequence of, that dispute, or whose dismissal, discharge or retrenchment has led to that dispute, but 
does not include any such person— 


(i) who is subject to the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950), or the Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950), or the 
Navy Act, 1957 (62 of 1957); or 


(ti) who is employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a prison; or 
(iii) who is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity; or 
(iv) who, being employed in a supervisory capacity, draws wages exceeding ten thousand rupees per 


mensem or exercises, either by the nature of the duties attached to the office or by reason of the 
powers vested in him, functions mainly of a managerial nature. 


Learned Counsel for Management has relied on judgment of Hon’ble High Court of Bombay in the case of 
Union Carbide (India) Ltd. V.s. Ramesh Kumbla and Others reported in MANU/MH/0073/1999 and 
another judgment of the same High Court in the case of Union Carbide (India) Ltd. V.s. D. Samuel 
and Others reported in MANU/MH/1713/1998. In these two cases, after analyzing the judgment of various 
High Courts and Hon’ble Supreme Court, the Single Bench of Hon’ble Bombay High Court has summarized 
the principles on the basis of which it is to be decided whether the Workman is in supervisory capacity or 
not. These tests mentioned in Para 34 and 35 of the Judgment are being reproduced as follows: 


Para-34, In so far as the Apex Court is concerned, some of the tests laid down are: 
(1) Designation is not material but what is important is the nature of work. 
(2) Find out the dominant purpose of employment and not any additional duties the employee 


may be performing. 


(3) Can he bind the Company/employer to some kind of decisions on behalf of the 


Company/employer. 
(4) Has the employee power to direct or oversee the work of his subordinates. 
(5) Has the power to sanction leave or recommend it; and 


(6) Has he the power to appoint, terminate or take disciplinary action against workmen. 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 995 


Para-35. From the judgment of this Court and the other High Courts some of the tests apart 
from what the Apex Court has stated are: 


(a 


~a 


Whether the employee can examine the quality of work and whether such work is performed in 
satisfactory manner or not; 


(b) Does the employee have powers of assigning duties and distribution of work; 

(c) Can he indent material and distribute the same amongst the workmen; 

(d) Even though he has no authority to grant leave does he have power to recommend leave; 
(e) Are there persons working under him; 

(f) Has he the power to supervise the work of men and not merely machines; 

(g) Dos he mark the attendance of other employees; 

(h) Does he write the confidential reports of his subordinates. 


Though, in his petition, the petitioner has alleged that he was not working in supervisory or Managerial 
capacity as he stated in his affidavit as his examination in chief but he never appeared for cross-examination with 
respect to his affidavit, hence his affidavit will never be read in support of his allegations on this petition. 


As it is evident from his appointment letter, his job has not been specified. He was appointed as Cluster In- 
charge in the Operation and Maintenance Department as Senior Executive Band F. There is no circular or standing 
order applicable with the Management, filed from the side of petitioner as regards to the responsibilities for the said 
post, hence keeping in view his pay structure he cannot be held to be workman under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


Since, the petitioner has been held not to be a workman under Section 2(s) of the Act; his claim is not 
cognizable by this Tribunal in this Act. 


Accordingly the petition fails. 
ORDER 
Petition dismissed. 
No order as to cost.

In view of the above said facts the claimant/workman has not field any statement of claim/ evidence in support of his 
case on affidavit, in spite of several opportunities given to him and taking into consideration the law as laid by the 
Hon'ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj Industries v. Labour Court (1) and others 1981 (29) FLR 194 as under: 


“It is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove illegality of the 
order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a workman 
raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file written statement 
before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must also produce evidence 
to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce evidence, the dispute referred 
by the State Government cannot be answered in favour of the workman and he would not be entitled to any relief.” 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (I), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (118) FLR 1164 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., V.K. Raj 
Industries v. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1984 (49) FLR 38 and 
Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led by or on behalf of the 
workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In such a situation it is not 
necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to establish an allegation 
made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would fail if no evidence is led.”

And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2010 (126) FLR 519; 


The Second party/Union by its application dated 04.10.2022 (Received in this office on 3.3.2023) desired to withdraw 
the present dispute and prayed that the second party women be allowed to withdraw the dispute. 


The application is allowed. As such thee reference is disposed of for want of prosecution.

This petition under Section 2 (A) (2&3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 as amended by the Amendment 
Act, 2010 filed by the petitioner workman against his termination with the case that he was first appointed as Cluster 
Incharge with the Management vide order dated 25.02.2015 and was posted at Guna (M.P.). He successfully 
completed his probation period and thereafter, he was transferred from Guna to Shivpuri. As his work was nowhere 
supervisory or Managerial in nature, the Respondent No. 4 was the immediate Boss of the petitioner made some 
illegal demands which the petitioner showed inability to fulfil, he threatens the petitioner to spoil his career. The 
petitioner was transferred from Shivpuri to Bhatpara vide communication on e-mail received on 28.06.2017. He was 
directed to report at Bhatpara on 03.07.2017. The petitioner was sick at that time and was not in a position to join at 
the new place of his posting. He submitted his application for medical leave which was sanctioned by Authorities and 
he also requested for cancellation of his transfer which was not accepted. Since, his transfer was mala fide and in form 
of his victimization, he raised a dispute before the Conciliation Officer in State Government. The Management 
terminated his services vide order dated 27.09.2017 on the ground that they have lost confidence in the petitioner 
which amounts to misconduct. This termination was without any show cause notice or any charge sheet initiating 
Departmental Enquiry, hence it is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. This act of Management amounts to retrenchment of 
services of the petitioner. Hence is in violation of Section 25F and 25G of the Act. The petitioner has prayed that 
setting aside his termination as it is vitiated in law, he be reinstated with back wages and consequential benefits. 


Due to absence of Management, the petition proceeded ex-parte against them. The petitioner had filed 
affidavit as his examination-in-chief and proved Exhibit W-1 to W-9 to be referred to as and when required. 

During the proceedings, the Management appeared and on their application, order to proceed ex-parte was 
set-aside on cost. Their written statement of defense was taken on record and case proceeded. 


The Management has taken a case that, firstly, the petitioner is not a workman under Section 2-S of the Act 
because he was a cluster in-charge drawing wages more than 40,000/- per month and was responsible for execution, 
operation and maintenance in Managerial and administrative capacity and Secondly, he was absenting himself un 
authorizedly and wilfully without permission of the Management and did not report on the place which he was 
transferred, hence Management was left with no option but to terminate his services. 


The petitioner did not appear for cross-examination by Management, in the light of his affidavit 
examination in chief. Management did not file any affidavit rather they filed the appointment letter and termination 
letter of the petitioner. 


At the stage of argument also, none appeared for petitioner. I have heard argument of Learned Counsel 
Mr. Jaideep Bansal for Management and have gone through records. 


It is worth mentioning that during the proceedings, the Management for Bharti Infratel was taken over by 
Indus Towers Limited and they were substituted in place of Bharti Infratel during the proceedings. 


The main objection raised by Management with regards to Maintainability of the petition is that, the 
petitioner is not a Workman as defined under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


The relevant provisions are being reproduced as under: 


2(s) “workman” means any person (including an apprentice) employed in any industry to do any manual, 
unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, whether the terms of 
employment be express or implied, and for the purposes of any proceeding under this Act in relation to an 
industrial dispute, includes any such person who has been dismissed, discharged or retrenched in connection with, 
or as a consequence of, that dispute, or whose dismissal, discharge or retrenchment has led to that dispute, but 
does not include any such person— 


(i) who is subject to the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950), or the Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950), or the 
Navy Act, 1957 (62 of 1957); or 


(ti) who is employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a prison; or 
(iii) who is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity; or 


(iv) who, being employed in a supervisory capacity, draws wages exceeding ten thousand rupees per 
mensem or exercises, either by the nature of the duties attached to the office or by reason of the 
powers vested in him, functions mainly of a managerial nature.

Though, in his petition, the petitioner has alleged that he was not working in supervisory or Managerial 
capacity as he stated in his affidavit as his examination in chief but he never appeared for cross-examination with 
respect to his affidavit, hence his affidavit will never be read in support of his allegations on this petition. 


As it is evident from his appointment letter, his job has not been specified. He was appointed as Cluster In- 
charge in the Operation and Maintenance Department as Senior Executive Band F. There is no circular or standing 
order applicable with the Management, filed from the side of petitioner as regards to the responsibilities for the said 
post, hence keeping in view his pay structure he cannot be held to be workman under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


Since, the petitioner has been held not to be a workman under Section 2(s) of the Act; his claim is not 
cognizable by this Tribunal in this Act. 


Accordingly the petition fails.

As per letter dated 10/12/2020 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per 
Notification No. J-1(1-47)/2020-IR dt. 10/12/2020. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“क्या प्रबन्धन: संचालक; जवाहर नवोवय AAA, भोपात्र FART करामगार श्री राधाकिशन उर्फ राजेश आत्मज श्री 
मोतीनान को विनांक: 28/01/2018 Ht ऑवूयॉगिक विवाद अधिनियम की धारा 25- एफ़ का अनुपालन किए बिना सेवा से पृथक 
किया जाना UTA A हैं? यवि नहीं तो श्री राधाकिशन उर्फ राजेश किस अनुतोष को पाने का अधिकारी हैं?" 


The case of the workman is mainly that, he was appointed as Helper against the vacant post on permanent 
basis on 14.04.2001 and worked in the Mess of the school continuously till 28.01.2018, his services were dispensed 
with by the management without any notice or compensation. According to him, this action of management is unjust, 
illegal and arbitrary and is in violation of the Act. He raised a dispute in this respect before the concerned Labour 
Commissioner, the dispute could not be conciliated hence, this reference. He has prayed for setting aside his 
disengagement, he be reinstated with all back wages and benefits. 


Case of the management is mainly that firstly, they are an educational institution, hence this Tribunal lacks 
jurisdiction in this respect. Secondly, he was appointed as a daily wager helper in the Mess of school on 14.04.2001, 
his work was not sufficient. He was disengaged by management since he was a daily wager, engaged on as and when 
required basis and never completed 240 days in any year, no notice or compensation is required on his disengagement. 
Management has requested that the reference be answered against the workman. 


The workman did not appear and did not file any evidence or affidavit. Management filed an affidavit of its 
witness which is on cross-examination. 


None appeared for the workman at the stage of argument, I have heard Learned Counsel for management, 
Mr. D. S. Baghel. I have gone through the record as well. 


The initial burden to prove his case lies on the workman, in which he failed as he has not filed any 
affidavit or evidence, hence holding his claim not proved. 


Hence, on the basis of above discussion and findings, holding the claim of the workman not proved, the 
reference deserves to be answered against the workman and stands answered accordingly. 


No order as to cost.

As per letter dated 12/11/2018 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per 
Notification No. L-42012/122/2018 (IR(DU)) dt. 12/11/2018. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of the management of Director, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Bhopal in 
terminating the services of Shri Deepak Jana, Plumber w.e.f., 02.03.2017 who was working through M/s Security 
Solutions and Manpower Services w.e.f. 06.11.2012 is just and proper? If not, what relief the workman concerned 
is entitled to ?" 


The case of the workman is mainly that, the management of All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Bhopal 
issued and advertisement on 21.07.2012 for appointment on many posts, he applied for the post of Plumber and after 
selection, appointed with the Institute vide appointment letter dated 01.11.2012. He was promoted w.e.f. 01.01.2014 
on the post of Senior Plumber on a consolidated pay, he was relieved from the Office of Superintendent Engineer of 
the Institute to join Admin office vide order dated 03.02.2017 and worked there till 02.03.2017 when he was 
disengaged vide letter of management dated 02.03.2017, issued by outsourcing agency, M/s Security Solutions and 
Manpower Services which was not empowered to terminate his services because he was appointed by the Institute. He 
was not given any opportunity of hearing before his disengagement nor was he issued any notice or compensation 
which is against the Act hence, is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. He raised the dispute before the Regional Labour 
Commissioner (Central), the dispute could not be conciliated hence, this reference. He has prayed for setting aside his 
disengagement order dated 02.03.2017, he be reinstated with all back wages and consequential benefits. 


The management of the Institute has taken a case in their written statement of defense that the workman 
was never appointed by them as claimed by him, he was not an employee of the Institute rather he was employed by 
the sanctioned manpower agency, M/s Security Solutions and Manpower Services, which appointed him and deputed 
him with the Institute for a fixed tenure on consolidated remuneration. He was paid by the outsourcing agency, there 
is no employer-employee relationship between him and the Institute, his services were terminated by the outsourcing 
agency. The management of Institute has admitted that the advertisement was issued by them for recruitment on 
contractual and outsource basis on 21.07.2012 because the Rules were not finalized at that time and candidates were 
appointed on outsourcing basis, after finalization of Recruitment Rules, legal selection process was initiated and 
finalized. Outsourced employees filed petition challenging their relieving and also claimed regularization of their 
services before Central Administrative Tribunal which was dismissed. This order was upheld by Hon’ble High Court 
of M.P. and thereafter by Hon’ble Supreme Court of India. Thus, according to management of Institute, the workman 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 1007 
was an outsourced employee, appointed by the outsourcing agency on contract basis and was terminated by the 
outsourcing agency after expiry of contract. 


The outsourcing agency, M/s Security Solutions and Manpower Services, did not appear inspite of service of 
notice, hence the case proceeded ex-parte against them. 


In evidence, the workman did not file his affidavit, management filed an affidavit of its witness. The 
workman did not appear for cross-examination of the witness. 


None appeared for the workman at the stage of argument, hence argument of Learned Counsel, Mr. Gopi 
Chaurasia were heard by me on behalf of the Institute. He has filed written submission also which are part of the 
record. I have gone through the record as well. 


The reference itself is the issue for determination in the case in hand. 


The initial burden to prove his case lies on the workman, he has not filed any affidavit in this respect. 
Management of Institute has filed photocopies of appointment letter of the workman, his promotion letter which go to 
show that he was appointed by M/s Vema Hospitality Pvt. Ltd., on 01.11.2012 as a Plumber to work with the Institute 
and was promoted by M/s Security Solutions and Manpower Services as a Senior Plumber. He was disengaged on 
administrative ground by M/s Security Solutions and Manpower Services. 


There is no evidence on record to show that the workman was appointed by the management of Institute or 
he worked under the Institute as an employee of the Institute. Hence, the Institute has no relation with the engagement 
as well disengagement of the workman in the case in hand. 


The burden to prove that he was disengaged without notice or compensation is also on workman, in absence 
of any evidence to this effect, he is held to have failed in discharging his, this burden. 


Hence, on the basis of above discussion and findings, holding the claim of the workman not proved, the 
reference deserves to be answered against the workman and stands answered accordingly. 


No order as to cost.

1. Workman has filed the present claim petition under Section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(hereinafter called the Act) against her termination w.e.f. 27.10.2018 claiming reinstatement into service along with 
continuity of service and full back wages. 


2. It is maintained by the workman in the claim petition that that she was appointed as sweeper/safai 
karamchari on 16.08.2012 by respondent 10.1 at minimum wages prescribed by the Central Government. But the said 
minimum wages were never paid to her. Management has unlawfully deducted 12% EPF share, 1.75% ESI and 
Rs.300/- as TDS from her salary despite of the fact that her total wages comes under the ambit of tax free limit. She 
was working under respondent no.1 directly, but respondent no.1 in order to avoid its liability always shows her 
employment in record under different contractors, which tantamount to unfair labour practice. 


3. It is further maintained that workman including 200 other safai karamcharis of respondent no.1 raised the 
demand for non-deduction of TDS from the wages paid by respondent 10.1. However, their demand was not accepted. 
Other workers working under respondent 10.1 formed union and subsequently her services were dispensed with w.e.f. 
27.10.2018. It is also maintained that respondent 10.1 retained juniors in service and also made fresh appointments 
after termination of her services and no compensation was paid under Section 25F of the Act. Thus, there is violation 
of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act. Hence this petition. 


4. Notice of the petition was given to respondents. 


5. Respondent no.1 filed reply to the claim petition maintaining therein that the workman has not come to the 
Court with clean hands as she was appointed as sweeper by respondent no.2 (contractor) at minimum wage rate as 
prescribed by the Central Government. As per Government Policy dated 18.03.2011 (Ex.R-1), Non-Cantonment 
Military Stations have been authorized to outsource conservancy safaiwala. The answering respondent entered into 
contract with various private agencies for outsourcing of sweepers (safai karamcharis). In July 2018, the answering 
respondent entered into contract with M/s AA Foundation for safety and M/s Sunrise Facilitator Pvt. Ltd. through e- 
tendering for outsourcing of safai karamcharis to provide conservancy services in Chandi Mandir Military Station for 
the financial year 2018-19. Respondent no.2 submits bill for payment for the days the safai karamcharis performed 
their duties and answering respondent is only responsible to forward these bills to PCDA Western Command 
Chandigarh to release payment directly to the contractor’s account. Salary is paid to the workman by the contractor. 
Compliance of PF, ESI Rules etc. is carried out by the contractor as per contract agreement. Answering respondent 
has no responsibility of disbursement of wages and deduction of EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai 
karamcharis formed union in the headquarter, which is not permitted and also carried out demonstration inside the 
premises of Station Headquarter on 27.10.2018 and failed to perform her duties. Thereafter, answering respondent 
asked respondent no.2 to ask the workers to perform their duties. Answering respondent has no role or responsibility 
for termination services of the workman. There is no relationship of employer and employee between the answering 
respondent and the workman. In view of Army Headquarter Letter, the civilian employees of the answering 
respondent cannot organize themselves into trade unions as station headquarter is an administrative office of the 
Government of India. In spite of that, workman along with other safai karamcharis formed union unauthorizedly and 
indulge in unlawful activities. It is maintained that workman is the employee of contractor and therefore, termination 
is the prerogative of the contractor. It is prayed that the claim be dismissed. 


6. It is pertinent to mention here that respondent no.2 was proceeded ex parte on 07.05.2024. 
Evidence of workman:- 


7. In order to prove her case, workman examined herself as WW1 and tendered into evidence her affidavit 
WWI/A and has been cross examined by the AR for respondent 10.1. AR for workman closed the evidence on 
22.07.2024. 


Evidence of respondent no.1:- 


8. Respondent 10.1 examined Colonel K P Singh S/o Late Colonel P. P. Singh, OIC, Civic Cell, Station Head 
Quarter, Chandi Mandir Panchkula as MW1, who tendered into evidence his affidavit Ex.MWI/A along with 
documents Ex.R1 to Ex.R4. AR for respondent 10.1 closed the evidence on 29.01.2026.

2 Agreement with respondent no.2 05.07.2018 Ex.R-2

Submissions of workman:- 


9. While arguing the case, AR for workman contended that in this case, workman was appointed by respondent 
10.1 under a camouflage agreement with respondent 10.2. The workman was appointed directly by respondent no.1 
on 16.08.2012 as sweeper and her services were dispensed with on 27.10.2018 without any reason in violation of 
Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act as no compensation was paid to the workman and junior to her were retained in 
service and fresh appointment were made after termination of the workman. So far as the agreements between the 
respondent 10.1 & 2 are concerned, they are totally not tenable and is unfair labour practice. The work performed by 
the workman is of perennial in nature. The contractor was not having any license. The contractor has left after three 
months. No domestic inquiry was held before terminating the service of the workman, which is mandatory under 
the Act. 


Submissions of respondent no.1:- 


10. On the other hand, AR for respondent 10.1 contended that the workman was engaged by respondent 10.2 
(contractor) as per agreement executed between respondent 10.1 & 2 on outsource basis and there is no relationship of 
employer and employee between respondent 10.1 and the workman. Wages were paid by the respondent 10.2 10 the 
workman and there was no role of respondent 10.1 in appointing or terminating the services of the workman. 
Workman is employee of respondent no.2. If there is any violation of provision of the Act, then it is done by 
respondent no.2. As per Ex.R3, all dues were paid by the contractor with regard to EPF and ESI etc. The workman 
and other safai karamcharis formed union in the Headquarter, which is not permitted as per Ex.R4. Respondent no.1 
being the Government Agency, workman is trying to take benefit of her appointment by respondent no.2 and has filed 
a false claim after concealing material facts and claim of the workman is not maintainable. 


11. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


Findings:- 

12. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of workman 
as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per her claim 
petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing her duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. She was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring her to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 
Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532, has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman. However, MW1 Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent no.1 has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 7, 2026/फालगुन 16, 1947 1021 


16. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent no.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and she was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.1. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through 
contract labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a 
sub-contractor; 


18. The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 
1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the 


Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test 
is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and 
substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy 
human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic 
activity for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent 10.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and 
respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, 
respondent no.2 would be termed as industry. 


19. Workman in her deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of 
the Act. She also stated that she was appointed on 16.08.2012 and she was paid minimum wages prescribed by 
Central Government and was working with respondent no.1. She was not given any compensation before terminating 
her services on 27.10.2018. In her cross examination, she has further stated that her salary used to be credited in her 
bank account. But she has not placed on record any bank account, in which her salary was credited in order to enable 
this Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid 
salary by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent 10.1. Thus, workman was employee of respondent 10.2 and not of respondent 10.1 as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


20. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


21. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent no.1 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between respondent 
10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that the work 
performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating the services 
of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for compensation under 
Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely 
because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get 
employment with respondent no.1, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that 
regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is 
not employee of respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent 10.2 (contractor). 


22. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working with 
respondent no.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to her during the 
period of her stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered

on 17.08.2017 as sweeper and his services were dispensed with on 27.10.2018 without any reason in violation of 
Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act as no compensation was paid to the workman and junior to him were retained in

service and fresh appointment were made after termination of the workman. So far as the agreements between the 
respondent 10.1 & 2 are concerned, they are totally not tenable and is unfair labour practice. The work performed by 
the workman is of perennial in nature. The contractor was not having any license. The contractor has left after three 
months. No domestic inquiry was held before terminating the service of the workman, which is mandatory under 
the Act. 


Submissions of respondent no.1:- 


10. On the other hand, AR for respondent 10.1 contended that the workman was engaged by respondent 10.2 
(contractor) as per agreement executed between respondent 10.1 & 2 on outsource basis and there is no relationship 
of employer and employee between respondent 10.1 and the workman. Wages were paid by the respondent 10.2 to 
the workman and there was no role of respondent 10.1 in appointing or terminating the services of the workman. 
Workman is employee of respondent no.2. If there is any violation of provision of the Act, then it is done by 
respondent no.2. As per Ex.R3, all dues were paid by the contractor with regard to EPF and ESI etc. The workman 
and other safai karamcharis formed union in the Headquarter, which is not permitted as per Ex.R4. Respondent no.1 
being the Government Agency, workman is trying to take benefit of his appointment by respondent 10.2 and has filed 
a false claim after concealing material facts and claim of the workman is not maintainable. 


11. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


Findings:- 

12. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his 
claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 
Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532, has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman. However, MW1 Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


16. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent no.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2.
